prompt: How many eight-queen arrangements remain when rotations and reflections count as the same solution?
explanation: Eight queens can occupy an otherwise empty board without attacking one another in 92 arrangements. Treating rotations and reflections as the same leaves just 12.

prompt: What makes a knight’s tour a closed tour?
answers: The last square is a knight move from the first
It returns by retracing every move
explanation: A knight’s tour visits all 64 squares exactly once. In a closed tour, its final square is one knight move from its starting square.

prompt: Why is a closed knight’s tour impossible on a board with an odd number of squares?
answers: A knight cannot reach a corner
A closed tour requires a capture
The center square blocks the knight
explanation: Every knight move switches square color. That simple fact proves that a closed knight tour on a board with an odd number of squares is impossible.

prompt: Why can’t dominoes tile a chessboard after two opposite corners are removed?
answers: The remaining colors have unequal square counts
There are an odd number of remaining squares
explanation: Remove two opposite corners from a chessboard and 31 dominoes can no longer cover it. Both corners share a color; every domino must cover one square of each color.

prompt: How can a rook and pawn sometimes draw against a queen?
answers: Automatic threefold repetition at the start
explanation: In a fortress, the stronger side may have no way to make progress. Some carefully arranged rook-and-pawn fortresses hold against a queen despite the material deficit.

prompt: In the endgame called a trebuchet, why is it bad to be the player who has to move?
answers: Both kings are already in check
explanation: In a trebuchet position, two kings defend mutually attacked pawns. Whoever must move first loses a pawn: the turn itself becomes a disadvantage.

prompt: What makes Réti’s 1921 king study work?
answers: One diagonal route pursues a pawn and supports its own pawn
The king captures two pawns in one move
A rook sacrifices itself on the back rank
The defender castles out of danger
explanation: Réti’s 1921 study draws because a king approaches an enemy pawn and supports its own pawn along the same diagonal. Moving diagonally need not cost extra moves.

prompt: Why is promoting to a queen wrong in the Saavedra study?
answers: It leaves the king in check
It makes the promoted piece immobile
explanation: The Saavedra study requires promotion to a rook. Choosing a queen allows a stalemate trick; the less powerful piece keeps a winning threat alive.

prompt: How many 2×2 squares are contained in an 8×8 board?
explanation: There are 64 one-by-one squares, but also 49 two-by-two squares, 36 three-by-three squares, and so on. Add all eight sizes to get 204.

prompt: What is the goal of the five-queen domination problem?
answers: Place five queens without any attacks
Force mate against a bare king
explanation: Five queens suffice to attack or occupy every square on an otherwise empty 8×8 board. Four cannot do it. This is a domination problem, distinct from the eight-queens puzzle.

prompt: What is an opening transposition?
answers: Reaching the same position by a different move order
Promoting a piece back into a pawn
explanation: A move-order transposition reaches the same position through different moves. Opening names describe a route; the resulting position, side to move and available rights determine what can happen next.

prompt: What does a desperado piece try to do?
answers: Capture something useful before it is inevitably lost
Stay permanently on its starting square
Trade itself only for the enemy king
explanation: In a desperado combination, an already doomed piece captures something before disappearing. Its apparent sacrifice may recover material that would otherwise be lost.

prompt: What is the point of an interference sacrifice?
answers: Add a new legal move to a knight
explanation: An interference sacrifice places a piece on a line between two enemy pieces. Capturing it may obstruct a different defender, which is the point of a Novotny theme.

prompt: How can a waiting move win without making a direct threat?
answers: It leaves the opponent in zugzwang
It makes an illegal move legal
explanation: A waiting move in a composed problem can create zugzwang: it makes no direct threat, yet every legal reply gives something away.

prompt: Which corner should the defending king aim for against a rook pawn and a bishop that cannot guard its promotion square?
answers: The promotion corner not controlled by the bishop
Any square next to the attacking king
The center, regardless of the pawn
The corner controlled by the bishop
explanation: A bishop controls only one square color, so the wrong rook-pawn corner can be a draw even with an extra bishop and pawn. The defending king must actually reach the safe corner.

prompt: Why might a position listed as a win in an endgame database still be drawn in a tournament?
answers: The fifty-move rule may prevent completing the win
explanation: Seven-piece tablebases contain positions requiring more than 500 moves to mate with perfect resistance when the fifty-move rule is ignored. A theoretical win is not always a tournament win.

prompt: On which device did Pocket Fritz 4 win the 2009 Copa Mercosur?
explanation: Pocket Fritz 4 won the 2009 Copa Mercosur with 9½/10 while running on an HTC Touch HD. Its search speed was tiny beside desktop engines, showing the value of evaluation and software.

prompt: How did Alan Turing test Turochamp against Alick Glennie in 1952?
answers: He simulated the algorithm by hand
He ran it on Deep Blue
He used an internet chess server
explanation: Turing’s Turochamp algorithm was conceived before a suitable computer was available to him. He manually simulated it in a 1952 game against Alick Glennie.

prompt: How did players send their moves during the 1844 Washington–Baltimore match?
explanation: The 1844 correspondence match between Washington and Baltimore used the new electric telegraph. Moves traveled faster than mailed letters long before internet chess.

prompt: Which cities hosted the opposing teams in the 1945 USA–USSR radio match?
explanation: The 1945 USA–USSR radio match connected players in New York and Moscow. The Soviet team won 15½–4½ without the teams sharing a room.

prompt: Who won the 1962 Curaçao Candidates tournament without losing a game?
explanation: The 1962 Candidates tournament took place in Curaçao, with eight players meeting four times each. Tigran Petrosian won without losing a game.

prompt: In which year did Max Euwe become world champion?
explanation: Max Euwe earned a doctorate in mathematics in 1926, became world chess champion in 1935, and later served as FIDE president.

prompt: Which world champion wrote the philosophical work Kampf?
explanation: Emanuel Lasker earned a mathematics doctorate and wrote philosophical works, including Kampf. His chess title reign lasted from 1894 to 1921.

prompt: Who held the record for youngest grandmaster before Judit Polgár broke it in 1991?
explanation: Judit Polgár became a grandmaster in 1991 at 15 years and 4 months, younger than Fischer had been. She later reached eighth in the world on a FIDE rating list.

prompt: Why did players write down and seal their next move when a game stopped for the day?
answers: Commit to the next move before overnight analysis
Hide the game result from spectators
explanation: Before powerful portable engines, long games could be paused with a sealed move. Players and their teams analyzed overnight, making preparation part of the unfinished game.

prompt: What could happen if a sealed move was illegal or ambiguous?
answers: The player could lose when the envelope was opened
Both players received a new queen
The move was automatically replaced by castling
explanation: Under adjournment rules, an ambiguous or illegal sealed move could cost the game when the envelope was opened. Players had to record the exact move, not just an intention.

prompt: Which restriction applies to a legal Chess960 starting position?
answers: The king starts between the rooks
Both bishops start on light squares
The queen must start on d1
explanation: Chess960 has 960 legal starting arrangements: bishops must stand on opposite colors, and the king must be between the rooks. Not every shuffle qualifies.

prompt: Why doesn’t a simple strategy-stealing argument prove that White must win chess?
answers: An extra move can be harmful because of zugzwang
explanation: In the game-theory strategy-stealing argument, being able to imitate a first player does not prove chess is a win for White: zugzwang means an extra move can be harmful.

prompt: Why could White and Black use different names for the same square in descriptive notation?
answers: Names depended on each player’s perspective
Each player chose a private alphabet
explanation: Algebraic notation is a coordinate system, while older descriptive notation names squares from each player’s perspective. The same square could therefore have different descriptive names.

prompt: Which piece retained its familiar leap while the queen and bishop changed substantially?
explanation: While the queen and bishop changed dramatically as modern chess evolved, the knight’s familiar leap is inherited from much earlier forms of the game.

prompt: Why can opposite-colored bishops help an attacking side in a middlegame?
answers: The rival bishop cannot defend the attacker’s square color
The defending king loses its legal moves automatically
Opposite bishops make every position a draw
explanation: Opposite-colored bishop endgames often draw, but in a middlegame the attacking bishop can operate on squares its rival can never defend. Queens and exposed kings change the story.

prompt: What did Levitsky do after Marshall’s famous 23...Qg3 in 1912?
answers: Promoted a pawn to a knight
explanation: After Marshall’s 23...Qg3 in the 1912 Levitsky game, White resigned rather than capture the queen. The famous position is a threat calculation, not a queen blunder.

prompt: Which square was the destination of Nigel Short’s famous king walk against Timman?
explanation: Against Timman in 1991, Nigel Short walked his king from g1 through h2, g3, f4 and g5. Its destination helped finish an attack while queens remained on the board.

prompt: What was Claude Shannon counting when he estimated a number around 10¹²⁰ for chess?
answers: The exact number of legal board positions
The number of possible first moves
explanation: Shannon’s famous rough game-tree estimate is about 10¹²⁰. It is an estimate, not an exact count.

prompt: How many queens can one side theoretically have after promotions?
explanation: One side can theoretically have nine queens: the original plus eight promoted pawns.

prompt: Does an attack on a rook alone forbid castling with that rook?
answers: No, the king’s path and other castling conditions matter
Yes, any attack on the rook forbids it
Only if the rook is attacked by a bishop
Only if the rook has not moved
explanation: A rook being attacked does not by itself prevent castling.

prompt: Must the repeated positions be consecutive for a threefold-repetition claim?
answers: Only if both kings are in check
explanation: Threefold repetition can be claimed; the repeated positions need not be consecutive.

prompt: How many repetitions make a draw automatic under standard FIDE rules?
explanation: Fivefold repetition ends a standard game automatically under FIDE rules.

prompt: What happens if the same move delivers checkmate and reaches the automatic 75-move draw limit?
answers: An immediate draw regardless of mate
explanation: After 75 such moves by each side, the game is drawn; checkmate on the last move takes priority.

prompt: Which extra information matters when deciding whether two positions are identical for repetition?
answers: Side to move and castling/en-passant rights
The color of the board frame
explanation: Repetition also depends on whose turn it is and the available castling and en-passant rights.

prompt: Can two knights force checkmate against a bare king with best defense?
answers: Only if both knights began on b1
explanation: Two knights cannot force checkmate against a bare king with best defense.

prompt: Toward which corner does bishop-and-knight checkmate drive the king?
answers: A corner matching the bishop’s square color
A corner not controlled by the bishop
explanation: Bishop-and-knight mate drives the king toward a corner matching the bishop’s color.

prompt: Which region is associated with chaturanga, a major ancestor of chess?
explanation: Chess traces its roots to chaturanga in India, around the sixth century.

prompt: When did the modern long-range queen emerge in Europe?
explanation: The modern queen’s long-range movement emerged in Europe in the late fifteenth century.

prompt: In which year was Lucena’s early printed chess book published?
explanation: Lucena’s 1497 book is an early printed source for modern chess rules and positions.

prompt: When was the Staunton chess-piece design introduced?
explanation: The Staunton piece design was introduced in 1849 and named after Howard Staunton.

prompt: Who won the landmark London 1851 tournament?
explanation: Adolf Anderssen won London 1851, a landmark international chess tournament.

prompt: Who won the first Women’s World Championship in 1927?
explanation: Vera Menchik won the first Women’s World Championship in 1927.

prompt: How many grandmaster titles did FIDE award in its inaugural 1950 group?
explanation: FIDE awarded its first 27 grandmaster titles in 1950.

prompt: Who became the first woman awarded the open grandmaster title in 1978?
explanation: Nona Gaprindashvili became the first woman awarded the open GM title in 1978.

prompt: After how many games was the 1984–85 Karpov–Kasparov match stopped?
explanation: The 1984–85 Karpov–Kasparov title match was stopped after 48 games without a champion being decided.

prompt: How many moves did the 1989 Nikolić–Arsović draw last?
explanation: Nikolić–Arsović, Belgrade 1989, lasted 269 moves.

prompt: What can an endgame tablebase provide within its piece limit?
answers: The identity of an unknown player
explanation: An endgame tablebase can give exact results for positions within its piece limit.

prompt: Why can two players with the same rating in different rating systems be different in strength?
answers: Elo is relative to results within its pool
A rating measures the number of games alone
The board color determines the scale
explanation: Elo measures results within a player pool; different pools are not automatically equivalent.

prompt: Why don’t early world champions have FIDE ratings from their title reigns?
answers: Published FIDE Elo lists began much later
Champions were banned from rating lists
Only correspondence games were rated then
All their games ended in draws
explanation: Published FIDE Elo lists began long after the first world championship. Early champions have no title-era FIDE rating.

prompt: Which match reunited the split world championship in 2006?
explanation: Kramnik’s 2006 victory over Topalov reunited the split world championship.
